```{ojs}
//| echo: false
buildQuiz = function(id, title, questions) {
  const outer = html`<div id="${id}" style="margin:18px 0 24px 0;text-align:center;">
    <button style="
      display:inline-flex;align-items:center;gap:7px;
      background:linear-gradient(135deg,#667eea 0%,#764ba2 100%);
      color:#fff;border:none;padding:9px 22px;border-radius:50px;min-height:44px;
      font-size:.95em;font-weight:700;cursor:pointer;
      box-shadow:0 3px 12px rgba(102,126,234,.45);">
      <span style="font-size:1.1em;">📝</span> ${title}
      <span class="chevron" style="transition:transform .3s;">▼</span>
    </button>
    <div class="quiz-body" style="
      max-height:0;opacity:0;overflow:hidden;
      transition:max-height .5s cubic-bezier(.4,0,.2,1),opacity .4s ease,margin-top .3s ease;
      margin-top:0;text-align:left;">
      <button class="close-btn" style="
        display:block;margin:0 auto 10px auto;
        background:rgba(102,126,234,.12);color:#667eea;border:none;
        padding:5px 18px;border-radius:50px;font-size:.85em;min-height:36px;
        font-weight:600;cursor:pointer;">Hide Quiz</button>
      <p style="text-align:center;color:#718096;font-style:italic;font-size:.9em;margin-bottom:12px;">
        Select an answer for each question.</p>
    </div>
  </div>`;
  const toggle = outer.querySelector("button");
  const chevron = toggle.querySelector(".chevron");
  const body   = outer.querySelector(".quiz-body");
  const closeBtn = body.querySelector(".close-btn");
  function expand(){  body.style.maxHeight="3000px";body.style.opacity="1";body.style.marginTop="14px";chevron.style.transform="rotate(180deg)"; }
  function collapse(){ body.style.maxHeight="0";body.style.opacity="0";body.style.marginTop="0";chevron.style.transform="rotate(0)"; }
  toggle.onclick = () => body.style.maxHeight === "0px" || body.style.maxHeight === "" ? expand() : collapse();
  closeBtn.onclick = collapse;
  questions.forEach((qq, qi) => {
    const card = document.createElement("div");
    card.style.cssText = "background:#fff;color:#1e1b4b;border-radius:12px;padding:16px 20px;margin-bottom:14px;box-shadow:0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,.08);";
    card.innerHTML = `<p style="font-weight:700;margin:0 0 10px;color:#1e1b4b;">${qi+1}. ${qq.q}</p>`;
    const fb = document.createElement("div");
    fb.style.cssText = "border-radius:8px;font-size:.9em;transition:all .3s;";
    qq.options.forEach((opt, oi) => {
      const btn = document.createElement("button");
      btn.textContent = opt;
      btn.style.cssText = "display:block;width:100%;min-height:44px;text-align:left;padding:10px 14px;margin:6px 0;border:2px solid #e2e8f0;border-radius:8px;background:#fff;color:#1e1b4b;cursor:pointer;font-size:.95em;transition:border-color .2s,background .2s;";
      btn.onclick = () => {
        if(card.dataset.answered) return;
        card.dataset.answered = "true";
        card.querySelectorAll("button").forEach(b => { b.style.cursor="default"; });
        if(oi === qq.correct){
          btn.style.borderColor="#48bb78";btn.style.background="#f0fff4";
          fb.innerHTML = "✅ Correct! " + qq.explanation;
          fb.style.color="#276749";fb.style.background="#f0fff4";
        } else {
          btn.style.borderColor="#fc8181";btn.style.background="#fff5f5";
          card.querySelectorAll("button")[qq.correct].style.borderColor="#48bb78";
          card.querySelectorAll("button")[qq.correct].style.background="#f0fff4";
          fb.innerHTML = "❌ " + qq.explanation;
          fb.style.color="#9b2c2c";fb.style.background="#fff5f5";
        }
        fb.style.padding="10px 14px";fb.style.marginTop="8px";
      };
      card.appendChild(btn);
    });
    card.appendChild(fb);
    body.appendChild(card);
  });
  return outer;
}
```

# Evidence Review: Connect to the Performance Task

::: {.engage-box}
## 🌡️ The task all unit

**Write (and now argue out loud) how storms will change in frequency and intensity as global temperatures continue to rise.** At the end of each lesson, your PTO asked you to apply what you figured out. Every PTO task has the same **3 parts**:

| Part | What you do |
|---|---|
| **1. Variables** | Name the **independent variable** (what changes: global temperature) and the **dependent variable** (storm frequency or intensity) |
| **2. Evidence + model** | Fill the evidence table (evidence + which resource), then model how **energy and matter flow** in the storm and the **small-scale mechanisms** (molecules, density, condensation) |
| **3. Argument** | Claim **and** counterclaim, using historical data, the conditions storms need, climate model projections, and the **limits** (precision, reliability, assumptions) of those models |

Lessons: [Blizzards](unit5-blizzards.qmd) → [Paths of Severe Storms](unit5-storm-paths.qmd) → [Hurricanes](unit5-hurricanes.qmd) (plus the optional [Moon Phases](unit5-moon-phases.qmd)).
:::

Quick check before you start: in every PTO prompt, which is which?

## Connect to the Performance Task: Blizzards {#connect-blizzards}

::: {.evidence-box}
### ❄️ Lesson 5.1: Blizzards

**PTO prompts (pp. 9–14), choose one:**

<div class="pto-prompt"><b>Task 1:</b> Will the frequency of winter storms per year where you live increase, decrease, or stay the same as global temperatures increase in the future?<br><b>Task 2:</b> Will the intensity of winter storms where you live increase, decrease, or stay the same as global temperatures increase in the future?</div>

**What we figured out:**

- **Wind:** the Sun heats Earth unevenly. Warm air particles move faster and spread out, so warm air is **less dense** and rises (low pressure). Cold, dense air sinks (high pressure). **Air moves from high to low pressure**, and a bigger difference means **stronger wind**.
- **Precipitation:** rising air expands and cools. Water vapor **condenses** on tiny particles into cloud droplets and **releases heat**, which keeps the air rising. Snow forms when the air is **below freezing**.
- **Blizzards form at fronts**, where a cold, dry air mass meets a warm, moist air mass. The warm air is pushed up over the cold air, forming a **mid-latitude cyclone** (low pressure). The two key elements of a winter storm are **cold air** and **moisture**, plus **lift** at the front.
- **Winter Storm Jonas (January 2016)** brought record snow to NYC: **27.5 inches in Central Park**.
- **Historical data (1950–2010, Nov–Mar):** winter storm **intensity increased** at both mid- and high latitudes. **Frequency increased at high latitudes** but went **up and down at mid-latitudes** (where NYC is) before a big jump in the 2000s.
- **Climate models (IPCC WGI Interactive Atlas):** winter temperatures where mid-latitude cyclones form are projected to **rise**, and precipitation to increase. The Atlas combines **many models built on different data sets**, which makes its projections **more precise**.

📖 Review the lesson: [Blizzards](unit5-blizzards.qmd)
:::

Explore the *What is the Future of Winter Storms?* graphs from your packet.

```{ojs}
  });
}
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!): sample arguments

**Task 2 (intensity), the clearer case.** *Claim:* Winter storms in NYC will likely become **more intense** as temperatures rise. *Evidence:* mid-latitude winter storm intensity rose from about −1.25 (1950s) to about +0.87 (2000s) above average; the IPCC Atlas projects warmer, wetter winters. *Reasoning:* warmer air holds more water vapor, so storms carry more moisture; more condensation releases more heat, strengthening the low and producing heavier snow when it's still below freezing. *Counterclaim:* if winter air in NYC is often **above freezing**, that moisture falls as **rain**, not snow, so some storms will be less "snowy" even if they are stronger.

**Task 1 (frequency), the uncertain case.** The mid-latitude frequency data go up and down, warmer winters mean fewer days cold enough for snow, but more moisture helps storms form. A strong answer **weighs both** and may conclude we **can't be sure** frequency will change, then says what more data you'd need.
:::

::: {.student-task}

- Choose **Task 1 (frequency)** or **Task 2 (intensity)** of winter storms where you live.
- **Part 1:** write the independent and dependent variables.
- **Part 2:** fill the evidence table (evidence + resource, e.g. *What is the Future of Winter Storms?*, IPCC Atlas). Then draw a model of winter storm formation in the future: **energy and matter flow** (warm moist air, cold dry air, rising, condensing) and the **small-scale mechanisms** (particle motion, density, condensation releasing heat).
- **Part 3:** argue with a **claim and counterclaim**, using historical storm data, the conditions a winter storm needs, climate model projections, and the **limited precision and reliability** of the models.
- Self or peer assess with the *Blizzards 5E Arguing from Evidence Rubric*.
:::

## Connect to the Performance Task: Paths of Severe Storms {#connect-storm-paths}

::: {.evidence-box}
### 🧭 Lesson 5.2: The Paths of Severe Storms

**PTO prompt (pp. 15–16):**

<div class="pto-prompt">Will the frequency of winter storms per year where you live increase, decrease, or stay the same as global temperatures increase in the future?</div>

**What we figured out:**

- **The Sun's energy is most direct at the equator** and spreads out toward the poles, so surface air is warmest near the equator and coldest near the poles.
- **Air masses take on the properties of where they form:** cold and dry over northern land (from Canada), warm and moist over the ocean near 30° N (Gulf of Mexico, Atlantic).
- **Global winds:** air rises at the equator, sinks at 30° N/S, and moves from high to low pressure. The **Coriolis effect** bends winds to the **right** in the Northern Hemisphere.
- **Why so many blizzards in the US:** global winds carry polar air south and tropical air north, so they **collide over North America**. The **westerlies** (30°–60° N) then steer winter storms from **southwest to northeast**, like Winter Storm Jonas. Hurricanes form in the tropics, move west with the trade winds, then **curve northeast** in the westerlies.
- **Evaluate (*How will global wind patterns be affected by rising global temperatures?*):** a research article claims that as Earth warms, the **westerlies (and the storms they carry) will shift toward the poles**, based on how they moved in the past. Your packet then asks you to imagine the westerlies moving about **5° north** and re-rank the storm bands on four winter storm track maps (2014–15, 2016–17, 2018–19, 2019–20).

📖 Review the lesson: [Paths of Severe Storms](unit5-storm-paths.qmd)
:::

**Shift the storm bands.** Count the storm tracks in each latitude band on one of your packet's maps and type your counts below (the starting numbers are only a placeholder pattern, not real counts). Then move the westerlies north.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof u5cCounts = {
  const bands = ["45–50° N", "40–45° N", "35–40° N", "30–35° N", "25–30° N"];
  const start = [3, 8, 9, 5, 1];
  const box = html`<div class="u5c-bands u5c-card" style="background:#fff;color:#1a1a1a;border-radius:12px;padding:12px 14px;box-shadow:0 2px 10px rgba(0,0,0,.1);">
    <div style="font-weight:700;margin-bottom:6px;">Storms per band (your counts):</div></div>`;
  const inputs = bands.map((b, i) => {
    const row = html`<label style="display:flex;justify-content:space-between;align-items:center;gap:10px;padding:4px 0;border-bottom:1px solid #eceff1;">
      <span>${b}${b === "40–45° N" ? " 🗽 NYC" : ""}</span><input type="number" min="0" max="40" step="1" value="${start[i]}"></label>`;
    box.appendChild(row);
    return row.querySelector("input");
  });
  box.value = bands.map((b, i) => ({band: b, n: +inputs[i].value || 0}));
  inputs.forEach(inp => inp.oninput = () => {
    box.value = bands.map((b, i) => ({band: b, n: Math.max(0, +inputs[i].value || 0)}));
    box.dispatchEvent(new Event("input", {bubbles: true}));
  });
  return box;
}
viewof u5cShift = Inputs.range([0, 5], {label: "Westerlies shift north (°):", step: 5, value: 0})
```

```{ojs}
    .html(`<b>Ranking (most → fewest):</b> ${ranked}<br>` + (u5cShift === 0
      ? "Move the slider to shift the westerlies 5° north."
      : `<b>NYC band (40–45° N):</b> ${nyc.before} → ${nyc.n} storms (${diff > 0 ? "+" + diff + ", more" : diff < 0 ? diff + ", fewer" : "no change"}). ${u5cShift > 0 ? "Dashed marks show the counts before the shift. Bands farther north gain storms; the southernmost band loses them." : ""}`));
  return wrap.node();
}
```

<p style="font-size:.85em;">NYC sits at about 40.7° N, right on the edge between the 35–40° and 40–45° bands, so try your counts both ways. As your teacher guide notes, counts from four maps are a <b>small sample</b>, so different years can give different answers. That uncertainty is part of your argument.</p>

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
buildQuiz("u5c-sp-quiz", "🧭 Check Your Understanding — Paths of Severe Storms", [
  {
    q: "Why do so many winter storms form over the United States?",
    options: ["Global winds bring cold, dry polar air south and warm, moist tropical air north, so they collide over North America", "The US is closest to the Sun", "Storms only form over land", "The Coriolis effect is strongest over the US"],
    correct: 0,
    explanation: "Air masses from Canada and from the Gulf/Atlantic meet over North America. Where they collide, warm air is lifted at the front and a mid-latitude cyclone forms."
  },
  {
    q: "If the westerlies shift about 5° toward the pole, which places are most likely to get MORE winter storms?",
    options: ["Places just north of today's busiest storm band", "Places in the tropics", "Places just south of today's busiest band", "Nowhere: storms would disappear"],
    correct: 0,
    explanation: "The storm tracks move with the westerlies, so the busiest band moves north. Places north of it gain storms, and places to the south lose them. Whether NYC gains or loses depends on where the busiest band is now."
  }
])
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!): a sample argument

**Claim:** The frequency of winter storms in NYC may **stay about the same or decrease slightly**, but the evidence is uncertain.

**Evidence:** On the storm track maps, the busiest bands are usually the middle latitudes (about 35–45° N). Shifting the westerlies 5° north moves storms from the 35–40° band up into NYC's 40–45° band, but also moves NYC's storms into the 45–50° band. Mid-latitude winter storm frequency from 1950–2010 went up and down.

**Reasoning:** Winter storms form where cold and warm air masses collide, and the westerlies steer them. Warming shrinks the temperature difference between the equator and the poles and pushes the westerlies toward the poles, carrying the storm tracks with them.

**Counterclaim and limits:** The maps are only four years, counting tracks is imprecise, and the article's prediction **assumes the westerlies will follow the historic pattern**. A different count or more years of data could change the answer.
:::

::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your PTO: Paths of Severe Storms 5E (pp. 15–16)

- **Part 1:** independent variable (global temperature) and dependent variable (winter storms per year where you live).
- **Part 2:** evidence table: the research article's claim about the westerlies, your **band rankings before and after a 5° shift**, and earlier storm frequency data.
- **Part 3:** argue with a **claim and counterclaim**. You may add pictures (e.g., a map with the shifted bands). Consider historical frequency data, the conditions a winter storm needs, climate model projections, and **the reliability of the models** (what the article assumes).
- Self or peer assess with *The Paths of Severe Storms 5E Arguing from Evidence Rubric*.
:::

## Connect to the Performance Task: Hurricanes {#connect-hurricanes}

::: {.evidence-box}
### 🌀 Lesson 5.3: Hurricanes

**PTO prompts (pp. 17–22), choose one (use the Hurricanes and the Paths of Severe Storms lessons):**

<div class="pto-prompt"><b>Task 1:</b> Will the frequency of hurricanes per year where you live increase, decrease, or stay the same as global temperatures increase in the future?<br><b>Task 2:</b> Will the intensity of hurricanes where you live increase, decrease, or stay the same as global temperatures increase in the future?</div>

**What we figured out:**

- **Hurricanes need warm ocean water (more than about 80 °F, 27 °C)**, which evaporates and carries heat energy into the air. Rising humid air **condenses, releasing heat**, which powers more rising air and forms a low-pressure eye. Winds coming together force air up; light winds outside let it grow.
- **Seasons and places:** in the North Atlantic, hurricanes happen **June to November**, when sea surface temperatures are highest. They form in the tropics and curve northeast in the westerlies (from the Paths lesson).
- **Warmer air holds more water**, so storms drop **more rain** during each event (Elaborate). This doesn't mean more total rain every year.
- **Historical data:** the **total number** of hurricanes worldwide **slightly decreased** from 1990 to 2020 (trend line from about 51 to about 44 per year), but the trend is **not the same everywhere**: the NOAA map shows **more** tropical cyclones per year in the **North Atlantic** (1980–2018) and fewer in parts of the Pacific and Indian Oceans.
- **Strong hurricanes (Category 4 and 5) increased** in all six regions from 1975–1989 to 1990–2004, and the **percentage** of hurricanes reaching Category 4–5 rose (trend line from about 34% to about 42%).
- **Climate models:** sea surface temperatures where hurricanes form are projected to **rise**. The IPCC Atlas shows **1.5, 2, 3, and 4 °C** warming scenarios because its **assumptions** (emissions, population, technology, policy, land use, feedbacks) can vary a lot.

📖 Review the lesson: [Hurricanes](unit5-hurricanes.qmd)
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!): a sample argument

**Claim (Task 2):** Hurricanes reaching NYC will likely become **more intense** as global temperatures rise.

**Evidence:** North Atlantic Category 4–5 hurricanes rose from **16 (1975–1989) to 25 (1990–2004)**; the share of hurricanes reaching Category 4–5 rose from about 34% to 42%; the IPCC Atlas projects warmer sea surface temperatures in hurricane regions.

**Reasoning:** Warm ocean water is the hurricane's energy source. Warmer water means more evaporation, so more water vapor carries energy into the storm. When it condenses, it releases more heat, which lowers pressure and strengthens winds. Warmer air also holds more water, so each storm can drop more rain.

**Counterclaim and limits:** The total number of hurricanes worldwide slightly **decreased**, so frequency may not rise. Strong hurricanes rarely reach NYC (about 40.7° N), because cooler northern water weakens them. The Atlas projections depend on **assumptions** about future emissions.
:::

::: {.student-task}

- **Part 2:** evidence table (graphs from *What is the Future of Tropical Cyclones?*, the strong hurricane table, the IPCC Atlas). Model hurricane formation in the future: **energy and matter flow** (warm water → evaporation → rising, condensing air → released heat) and the **small-scale mechanisms**.
- **Part 3:** argue with a **claim and counterclaim**, using historical hurricane data, the conditions a hurricane needs (or needs to gain energy), climate model projections, and **the reliability of the model** (its assumptions).
- Use the *Final Argument Rubric* (in the [checklist below](#final-argument-checklist)).
:::

## Moon Phases and Hurricane Sandy {#moon-phases-and-hurricane-sandy}

::: {.key-idea}
### 🌕 Optional Moon Phases 3E: How does the moon contribute to storm severity?

- **Hurricane Sandy (October 29–30, 2012)** caused historic flooding in NYC partly because it hit during a **spring tide**: the full moon was on October 29.
- **Spring tides** happen at **new and full moon**, when the Sun, Moon, and Earth line up, so their pull adds up and high tides are **higher**. **Neap tides** (first and last quarter) have smaller tidal ranges.
- **For your argument:** storm damage depends on more than climate. **Timing with the tides** (and rising sea level from [Unit 4](../unit4-climate-change/unit4-past-and-future.qmd)) can make the same storm surge reach much farther. This 3E has no PTO page, but it's great evidence for a counterclaim or for the "limits" part of your argument.

📖 Review the lesson: [Moon Phases](unit5-moon-phases.qmd)
:::

# Return to the Anchor Phenomenon {#return-to-the-anchor-phenomenon}

::: {.engage-box}
## 🔁 It has felt like storms are getting worse. Does the data support that feeling, and will it continue?

At the start of the unit you watched *A Deadly Winter Storm Heads to the East Coast* and *Island of Puerto Rico destroyed by Hurricane Maria*, and studied maps of the 2018–19 and 2019–20 winter storm seasons and the 2018 and 2020 Atlantic hurricane seasons ([Unit Opening](unit5-opening.qmd)).

**Now review your ideas:** What causes hurricanes and blizzards? What patterns does the past and present data show? What does the data suggest about storms in the future?
:::

| Question | What the unit's evidence says |
|---|---|
| **What causes blizzards?** | Cold, dry and warm, moist air masses colliding at a front; rising air cools and condenses; big pressure differences make strong wind |
| **What causes hurricanes?** | Warm ocean water (> ~80 °F) evaporating; condensation releases heat that powers the storm |
| **Why here?** | Global winds bring air masses together over North America; the westerlies steer storms toward the Northeast |
| **More intense?** | Strong evidence: winter storm intensity and Category 4–5 hurricanes both increased; warmer air and water add more energy and moisture |
| **More frequent?** | Uncertain: mid-latitude winter storm frequency is mixed, global hurricane totals fell slightly while North Atlantic storms rose, and storm tracks may shift north |

# Final Performance Task {#final-performance-task}

::: {.engage-box}
## 🎤 How will storms change in our region as climate change continues?

**The future of storms is uncertain.** Our data show trends in winter storms and hurricanes over time, but other factors may change those paths. Not every region will be impacted in the same ways, and not all types of storms will change in the same ways.

**Your task:** prepare an **oral argument** about the **future frequency and intensity of hurricanes and winter storms in your region**. In class you will either **present it in groups** or debate it in a **Socratic seminar**. Working on your own? Write your argument with the planner below, then practice saying it out loud (record yourself if you can).
:::

## What Your Argument Must Include

| Be sure to include... | Evidence from |
|---|---|
| A **claim** for each: winter storm frequency, winter storm intensity, hurricane frequency, hurricane intensity, **in your region** | Your three PTO tasks |
| **At least 2 pieces of evidence for each claim** (data, simulations, models, or reputable data sets) | [Blizzards](#connect-blizzards), [Paths](#connect-storm-paths), [Hurricanes](#connect-hurricanes) |
| **Reasoning**: the conditions each storm needs and how warming changes them (energy and matter, molecules) | All three lessons |
| A **counterclaim**: evidence or ideas that point the other way | Mixed frequency data, rain vs. snow, westerlies shift, tides |
| **Limits of models**: precision, reliability, assumptions | IPCC Atlas (many models; scenarios), article's assumption about the westerlies |

::: {.claim-box}
### 📌 CLAIM
Make one clear prediction for each storm type and each variable. Example starter: "As global temperatures rise, winter storms in NYC will become ___ intense, because ___."
:::

::: {.evidence-box}
### 📊 EVIDENCE
Pick **specific numbers**: mid-latitude winter storm intensity −1.25 → +0.87 (1950s → 2000s); North Atlantic Category 4–5 hurricanes 16 → 25; Cat 4–5 share ~34% → ~42%; global hurricane totals ~51 → ~44 per year; the band rankings from your 5° westerlies shift; projected warming of 1.5–4 °C by 2100.
:::

::: {.reasoning-box}
### 🧠 REASONING
Connect each number to the mechanism: *Warmer air holds more water vapor, so storms have more moisture. When water vapor condenses, it releases heat, which makes air rise faster, lowers the pressure, and strengthens the wind. Therefore warmer oceans and air give storms more energy.* Use "because" and "therefore."
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
u5cPlanner = {
  const KEY = "u5c-planner-v1";
  let saved = {};
  try { saved = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(KEY) || "{}") || {}; } catch (e) { saved = {}; }
  const fields = [
    {id: "region", label: "📍 Your region (city or area, and its latitude)", rows: 1},
    {id: "ivdv", label: "🔬 Independent variable / dependent variable(s)", rows: 2},
    {id: "claim", label: "📌 CLAIMS: winter storm frequency, winter storm intensity, hurricane frequency, hurricane intensity (increase, decrease, stay the same, or uncertain?)", rows: 4},
    {id: "evidence", label: "📊 EVIDENCE: at least 2 pieces for each claim, with the resource each came from", rows: 5},
    {id: "reasoning", label: "🧠 REASONING: the conditions each storm needs, how warming changes them, energy and matter flow, small-scale mechanisms (use because / therefore)", rows: 5},
    {id: "counter", label: "↔️ COUNTERCLAIM: evidence or ideas that point the other way, and why your claim is still stronger (or why you're unsure)", rows: 4},
    {id: "limits", label: "⚖️ LIMITS OF MODELS: precision (how many models agree), reliability (assumptions like emissions or westerlies following past patterns), small samples", rows: 4},
    {id: "seminar", label: "🗣️ For the seminar: a question you'd ask a classmate who disagrees, and what more data you'd want", rows: 3}
  ];
  const focusOpts = ["All four (winter storms + hurricanes, frequency + intensity)", "Winter storms only", "Hurricanes only"];
  const box = html`<div class="u5c-planner u5c-card" style="background:#fff;color:#1a1a1a;border-radius:14px;padding:16px;box-shadow:0 2px 12px rgba(0,0,0,.12);border-top:6px solid #0277bd;"></div>`;
  const focusWrap = html`<label style="display:block;font-weight:700;margin-bottom:10px;">🎯 Focus
    <select style="display:block;min-height:44px;margin-top:4px;border:2px solid #b3e5fc;border-radius:8px;padding:6px;background:#fff;color:#1a1a1a;">${focusOpts.map(f => html`<option>${f}</option>`)}</select></label>`;
  const focus = focusWrap.querySelector("select");
  if (saved.focus) focus.value = saved.focus;
  box.appendChild(focusWrap);
  const areas = {};
  fields.forEach(f => {
    const lab = html`<label style="display:block;font-weight:700;margin:10px 0 4px;">${f.label}
      <textarea rows="${f.rows}" style="display:block;margin-top:4px;border:2px solid #b3e5fc;border-radius:8px;padding:8px;font:inherit;font-weight:400;background:#fff;color:#1a1a1a;"></textarea></label>`;
    const ta = lab.querySelector("textarea");
    ta.value = saved[f.id] || "";
    areas[f.id] = ta;
    box.appendChild(lab);
  });
  const status = html`<div style="font-size:.85em;color:#00695c;min-height:1.2em;margin-top:6px;"></div>`;
  const preview = html`<div style="white-space:pre-wrap;background:#e1f5fe;color:#1a1a1a;border-radius:8px;padding:12px;margin-top:10px;font-size:.92em;display:none;"></div>`;
  const btnStyle = "min-height:44px;padding:8px 16px;border:none;border-radius:50px;font-weight:700;cursor:pointer;margin:8px 8px 0 0;";
  const bPrev = html`<button style="${btnStyle}background:#0277bd;color:#fff;">👀 Preview outline</button>`;
  const bCopy = html`<button style="${btnStyle}background:#1a237e;color:#fff;">📋 Copy outline</button>`;
  const bClear = html`<button style="${btnStyle}background:#eceff1;color:#37474f;">🗑️ Clear</button>`;
  const outline = () => [`FOCUS: ${focus.value}`, ...fields.map(f => `\n${f.label.replace(/^\S+\s/, "").split(":")[0].toUpperCase()}:\n${areas[f.id].value}`)].join("\n");
  const save = () => {
    const data = {focus: focus.value};
    fields.forEach(f => data[f.id] = areas[f.id].value);
    try { localStorage.setItem(KEY, JSON.stringify(data)); status.textContent = "Saved in this browser."; } catch (e) { status.textContent = "Couldn't save in this browser. Copy your outline before leaving."; }
  };
  box.addEventListener("input", save);
  focus.addEventListener("change", save);
  bPrev.onclick = () => { preview.textContent = outline(); preview.style.display = "block"; };
  bCopy.onclick = async () => {
    const text = outline();
    try { await navigator.clipboard.writeText(text); status.textContent = "Copied! Paste it into your notes or PTO."; }
    catch (e) { preview.textContent = text; preview.style.display = "block"; status.textContent = "Copy isn't available here. Select the outline below and copy it."; }
  };
  bClear.onclick = () => {
    fields.forEach(f => areas[f.id].value = ""); preview.style.display = "none";
    try { localStorage.removeItem(KEY); } catch (e) {}
    status.textContent = "Cleared.";
  };
  const row = html`<div></div>`;
  row.append(bPrev, bCopy, bClear);
  box.append(row, status, preview);
  return box;
}
```

# Unit Summary

| Big idea | What the evidence shows |
|---|---|
| **The phenomenon** | It has felt like storms are getting worse (Winter Storm Jonas, Hurricane Maria, Hurricane Sandy). Does the data agree, and will it continue? |
| **Blizzards** | Uneven heating makes pressure differences and wind; rising air cools and condenses into snow at fronts where cold and warm air masses meet. Winter storm intensity rose from 1950 to 2010; mid-latitude frequency was mixed |
| **Paths of Severe Storms** | Global winds and the Coriolis effect bring air masses together over North America and steer storms southwest → northeast. A warming world may shift the westerlies and storm tracks toward the poles |
| **Hurricanes** | Warm ocean water powers hurricanes through evaporation and condensation. Global totals fell slightly, but North Atlantic storms and Category 4–5 hurricanes increased |
| **Moon Phases (optional)** | Spring tides at new and full moon raise high tides; Sandy's surge on a spring tide made NYC flooding worse |
| **The future** | Intensity: likely to increase. Frequency: uncertain and regional. Models are more precise when many agree, but their reliability depends on assumptions about the future |

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
function buildUnit5Quiz(id, title, questions) {
  const outer = html`<div id="${id}" style="font-family:'Inter',sans-serif; max-width:720px; margin:18px auto;"></div>`;
  const header = html`<div style="background:linear-gradient(135deg,#1a237e 0%,#0277bd 100%);color:#fff;border-radius:14px 14px 0 0;padding:18px 24px;">
    <div style="font-size:1.1em;font-weight:700;display:flex;align-items:center;gap:8px;color:#fff;"><span style="font-size:1.2em;">📝</span> ${title}</div>
    <div style="font-size:0.85em;opacity:0.9;margin-top:4px;color:#fff;">Select an answer for each question.</div>
  </div>`;
  const body = html`<div style="border:1.5px solid #b3e5fc;border-top:none;border-radius:0 0 14px 14px;overflow:hidden;background:#f3faff;padding:16px;"></div>`;
  questions.forEach((qq, qi) => {
    const card = document.createElement("div");
    card.style.cssText = "background:#fff;color:#1e1b4b;border-radius:12px;padding:16px 20px;margin-bottom:14px;box-shadow:0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,.08);";
    card.innerHTML = `<p style="font-weight:700;margin:0 0 10px;color:#1e1b4b;">${qi+1}. ${qq.q}</p>`;
    const fb = document.createElement("div");
    fb.style.cssText = "border-radius:8px;font-size:.9em;transition:all .3s;";
    qq.options.forEach((opt, oi) => {
      const btn = document.createElement("button");
      btn.textContent = opt;
      btn.style.cssText = "display:block;width:100%;min-height:44px;text-align:left;padding:10px 14px;margin:6px 0;border:2px solid #e2e8f0;border-radius:8px;background:#fff;color:#1e1b4b;cursor:pointer;font-size:.95em;transition:border-color .2s,background .2s;";
      btn.onclick = () => {
        if(card.dataset.answered) return;
        card.dataset.answered = "true";
        card.querySelectorAll("button").forEach(b => {
          b.style.cursor="default"; b.style.borderColor="#e2e8f0"; b.style.background="#f8fafc"; b.style.color="#475569";
        });
        const correctBtn = card.querySelectorAll("button")[qq.correct];
        correctBtn.style.borderColor="#48bb78";correctBtn.style.background="#f0fff4";correctBtn.style.color="#276749";correctBtn.style.fontWeight="700";
        if(oi === qq.correct){
          fb.innerHTML = "✅ Correct! " + qq.explanation;
          fb.style.color="#276749";fb.style.background="#f0fff4";
        } else {
          btn.style.borderColor="#fc8181";btn.style.background="#fff5f5";btn.style.color="#9b2c2c";btn.style.fontWeight="700";
          fb.innerHTML = "❌ " + qq.explanation;
          fb.style.color="#9b2c2c";fb.style.background="#fff5f5";
        }
        fb.style.padding="10px 14px";fb.style.marginTop="8px";
      };
      card.appendChild(btn);
    });
    card.appendChild(fb);
    body.appendChild(card);
  });
  outer.appendChild(header);
  outer.appendChild(body);
  return outer;
}
```
